newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian housing seen on track for stronger 1997.
newsitem.headline: Australian housing seen on track for stronger 1997.

text.p: Australia's housing sector remains on track for gradual recovery through 1997, despite data on Thursday showing a fall in building approvals during March, economists said.
Official data showed a 1.8 percent fall in March building approvals, against median forecasts of a 2.0 percent rise.
While the second consecutive monthly fall was disappointing, those looking for improving strength in the housing sector took heart from a 4.1 percent rise in the number of private sector houses.
"The building sector is still trending up and today's figures was but a hiccup on a steady growth path," Colonial State Bank group economist Hans Kunnen said.
March's fall and the 3.7 percent fall in February were seen as corrections to January's massive 10.4 percent rise, which was driven by a 37 percent increase in units and townhouses.
"Small declines in building approvals over the last two months need to be put into proper perspective," Axiom Funds Management senior economist Matthew Drennan said.
While the monthly numbers can be affected by approvals of large multi-dwelling buildings -- as was the case in January's rise -- the data still shows a steady improvement overall.

In the March quarter, monthly building approvals averaged out to 11,655, a 5.3 percent increase on the 11,072 monthly average of the December quarter and 14.1 percent above the monthly average of 10,219 posted in the March quarter of 1996.
This was consistent with an improvement in factors seen as traditional strong influences on the housing cycle.
"Housing affordability is at record levels and immigration has been much higher than generally appreciated over the last 12 months," Axiom's Drennan said.
Building approvals are seen as a leading indicator of not only the housing sector, but also the economy more generally.

Building approvals should lead to new contstruction, which in turn should boost employment, but it also has spin-off effects for manufacturers of housing materials and also for retail spending as the owners furnish their new dwellings.
However, unlike previous housing cycles economists were expecting the 1997 upswing to be more more gradual given that the economy was not consitently strong across the board.
Signs of moderate strength were an indication that official interest rates were on hold, rather than rising or falling.
"We are not in store for a building boom, but the sector will play its part in an improved economy in the second half of the year," Colonial's Kunnen said.
